L3-01.why: Rhetoric/style set: C is vague filler ('have an effect'), D is a flat simile, B unknown. A is the only option that carries a fully worked parallel comparison (invite/invites) with a concrete vehicle, which is the shape ACT rewards when the alternatives are progressively weaker versions of the same image. Solved by ranking the four for vividness, not by any grammar rule.

L3-02.why: Reflexive-pronoun set. 'theirselves' is nonstandard and eliminable outright; that leaves itself / himself / No Change. I cannot see the antecedent, so this is a coin flip between a singular thing and a singular man. Picked 'found itself' only because ACT pronoun-agreement items more often hinge on a collective/institutional singular antecedent being wrongly pluralised. Essentially a guess.

L3-03.why: Yes/No purpose item, 2-2 split. The two No's describe an essay with no broader point; the two Yes's differ in what the essay is about. C is the archetypal key shape for this question type: a concrete difficulty producing a wider insight. A narrows the essay to a portrait of a named person, which is usually the distractor that mistakes a detail for the subject.

L3-04.why: Punctuation. The trailing comma is constant across all four, so the only live question is what precedes 'within a year'. C ('; and') is eliminable: a semicolon before a coordinating conjunction is never right on the ACT. Between A and B I took the no-extra-comma option, on the default that ACT punishes unnecessary interrupting commas around a short prepositional phrase. Low confidence because without the sentence I cannot tell whether the phrase is genuinely parenthetical, in which case B's matched pair wins.

L3-05.why: Transition item with no context whatsoever. 'Otherwise' is a near-dead option on the ACT and I dropped it; 'Meanwhile' requires simultaneity I cannot verify. Picked 'As a result' as the most frequent causal key. This is a guess and I expect transitions to be at chance blind.

L3-06.why: Classic conciseness set: A adds a self-evident gloss ('which is not long'), D inflates 'days' into "days' worth of time", and No Change is presumably the wordy original the alternatives are trimming. B is the only option with nothing redundant in it. The shortest non-ungrammatical option wins in redundancy sets.

L3-07.why: Register/precision set. D is padded ('in its entirety'), A is vague ('the whole thing') and loses the referent. C names the object plainly. Weak because the pattern here does not cleanly isolate one survivor the way L3-06 and L3-15 do, and No Change could easily be the plain version with C as its synonym.

L3-08.why: Sentence-placement item. The four options are pure coordinates (Point A-D, paragraphs 2-5) with no semantic content at all, so the option set cannot discriminate. Pure guess; chose a mid-essay placement because placement keys skew away from the extremes. Recording this as a guess, not a pick.

L3-09.why: Add/replace-a-closing-sentence item. C is self-contradictory in spirit (lease to whichever bidder comes first) and D asks for something unrelated to the proposal, so both read as distractors. That leaves No Change vs B, and B introduces a new directive to skeptics that a conclusion would not normally add. Chose No Change by elimination, but with no essay I cannot check that the existing sentence is actually on-topic.

L3-10.why: Register triplet: A is inflated jargon ('cease all sonic emissions'), C is slangy and hedged ('quiet-ish'), leaving B as the plain idiomatic phrase. Same mechanism as L3-15: when one option is pompous and one is colloquial, the neutral middle is the key and No Change is the flawed original.

L3-11.why: Yes/No purpose item. A invents a comparison (wave vs battery power) that no single-subject essay would sustain; D reduces it to harbor history. B and C are the real pair and they are exact inverses about what is foreground. Picked C because the mention of 'Marrow' as a named engineer in B's own wording signals the essay is built around her, making 'mechanism treated briefly' the accurate description.

L3-12.why: Verb-form set. B ('having built up') is the standard participle distractor that would leave a fragment, so it is eliminable. Among No Change, future perfect, and simple present I have no context for the timeframe. Picked the simple present as the most common resolution of a tense-consistency item. Guess.

L3-13.why: sink/sank/sunk set. 'had sunken' is nonstandard and 'sunk' as a bare simple past is the classic error, so both are eliminable. That leaves No Change against an unmotivated passive ('was sunk'); an unprompted shift to passive is rarely the key, so No Change. Decided entirely by eliminating the two known-bad forms.

L3-14.why: Yes/No purpose item. C ('history of broomstacking') is too narrow to be an essay's subject and reads as a trap on one detail; A and D are the No pair. B is the only option whose description contains both halves a goal statement about traditions-and-survival would require (describes the customs AND ties them to the game persisting), which is the usual signature of the key in Yes/No items.

L3-15.why: Register triplet again: A is inflated ('demonstrably superior quality'), D is colloquial and hedged ('pretty decent, I guess'), leaving C as the concrete, tonally neutral option. Same mechanism as L3-10.
